title: Gap Characterization of ⟨2,5⟩
content: `representable_iff` is the headline lemma: a natural number is a non-negative combination $2a + 5b$ iff it is neither $1$ nor $3$. The forward direction is immediate (`omega` knows $2a+5b$ can never equal $1$ or $3$). The reverse is an elementary parity split: even $n = 2k$ uses $a=k, b=0$; odd $n = 2k+1$ with $n \notin \{1,3\}$ forces $k \ge 2$, so $n = 2(k-2) + 5$. This single fact drives the entire gap structure.
mathContext: The numerical semigroup generated by two coprime integers $p, q$ is $\{pa + qb : a,b \ge 0\}$. Its complement in ℕ (the 'gaps' or 'holes') is finite, of size $(p-1)(q-1)/2$. For $p=2, q=5$ this is $(1)(4)/2 = 2$ gaps, namely $\{1, 3\}$.

title: Frobenius Number 3 = 2·5 − 2 − 5
content: `frobenius_two_five` shows $3$ is non-representable while every $m > 3$ is representable — i.e. $3$ is the largest non-representable integer, the Frobenius number of ⟨2,5⟩. `frobenius_value` records that this matches the classical Sylvester formula $g(p,q) = pq - p - q$ for coprime $p,q$: here $2 \cdot 5 - 2 - 5 = 3$.
mathContext: Sylvester (1882) proved that for coprime $p, q$ the largest integer not representable as $pa+qb$ ($a,b \ge 0$) is $pq - p - q$. The number of non-representable integers (gaps) is exactly $(p-1)(q-1)/2$.

title: Line-Count Deficit: Generators Are Triples and Quadruples
content: `lineDeficit k = C(k,2) − 1` is the number of distinct lines lost when $k$ configuration points are made collinear: their $\binom{k}{2}$ pairs collapse to one line. `lineDeficit 2 = 0` (an ordinary line costs nothing), `lineDeficit 3 = 2`, `lineDeficit 4 = 5` — so the smallest rich lines, a triple and a quadruple, are exactly the generators $2$ and $5$ of the semigroup. `representable_via_triples_quadruples` confirms every representable deficit is realized using triples and quadruples alone.
mathContext: Replacing $k$ general-position points by $k$ collinear points changes the line contribution from $\binom{k}{2}$ (one line per pair) to $1$, a reduction of $\binom{k}{2} - 1$. Disjoint collinear groups contribute additively, so achievable deficits form the numerical semigroup generated by $\{\binom{k}{2}-1 : k \ge 3\} = \{2,5,9,14,\dots\}$; but $\langle 2,5\rangle$ already fills all but $\{1,3\}$.

title: Exactly C(n,2)−1 and C(n,2)−3 Are Forbidden
content: Translating deficits $d$ back to line counts $\binom{n}{2} - d$, `forbidden_line_counts` proves that for $n \ge 4$ the only unreachable counts at the top of the range are $\binom{n}{2}-1$ (deficit $1$) and $\binom{n}{2}-3$ (deficit $3$), while $\binom{n}{2}$, $\binom{n}{2}-2$ and $\binom{n}{2}-4$ are reachable. This is exactly the Erdős–Salamon gap set. `exactly_two_gaps` records that the forbidden set $\{1,3\}$ has cardinality $2$.
mathContext: Erdős–Salamon (1988): for large $n$ the achievable distinct-line counts are $\{1\} \cup ([n, \binom{n}{2}] \setminus \{\binom{n}{2}-1, \binom{n}{2}-3\})$. The two forbidden values are precisely the images of the two semigroup gaps $1$ and $3$ under $d \mapsto \binom{n}{2} - d$.

title: Honest Scope: Arithmetic Core Only
content: This file proves the number-theoretic reason the gap set is $\{1,3\}$ and nothing else. It does NOT prove geometric realizability — that disjoint collinear triples and quadruples can actually be embedded in the plane to realize each deficit — which is the genuine geometric content carried by the parent file's axioms. Nor does it resolve OQ-01's literal question, the exact Erdős–Salamon threshold $N_0$. The result is fully machine-checked (0 sorries, 0 axiom declarations; only propext / Classical.choice / Quot.sound).
mathContext: Separating the arithmetic (which values are combinatorially possible) from the geometry (which configurations are realizable in ℝ²) is standard in extremal combinatorics: the semigroup argument bounds the gaps, while Sylvester-Gallai-type constructions establish realizability.
